title: Pluperfect and other compound tenses
objectives: I can use the pluperfect (tinha feito) to place one past action before another.
I can form and use the future perfect (terei feito) and the conditional perfect (teria feito).
I can use the compound subjunctive tenses (tenha feito, tivesse feito, tiver feito) and build unreal past conditionals such as Se eu tivesse sabido, teria ido.
I can express regret and missed opportunities with devia ter, podia ter and se ao menos.
I can tell a life story or a sequence of historical events with a clear chronology.
I can explain why the auxiliary forms and the history words of this unit are spelled and accented as they are.

vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb: the se is the reflexive pronoun from the daily routine lesson, and the thing regretted follows de (arrepender-se de algo). In speech the pronoun goes before the verb: me arrependo. The rr is the strong r sound, the en before d is a nasal vowel, and the se after the hyphen is said si. The infinitive ends in r, so the stress is on der: ar-re-pen-DER-si.

example.target: Eu me arrependo de não ter aprendido inglês mais cedo.
example.source: I regret not having learned English earlier.
example.source_literal: I myself repent of not to-have learned English more early.

vocabulary.note: The noun made from arrepender-se with the suffix -imento, which names the act or result of a verb (acontecer gives acontecimento in the same way). The word ends in o, so the stress is on the second to last syllable: ar-re-pen-di-MEN-to. The rr is the strong r and both en syllables are nasal.

example.target: O maior arrependimento dele foi não ter viajado quando era jovem.
example.source: His greatest regret was not having traveled when he was young.

vocabulary.note: A cognate of English lament, but weaker: it says you are sorry about something, often something that happened to someone else. Lamento alone is a polite reply to bad news. For your own action it takes a compound infinitive (Lamento ter dito isso); for someone else's action it takes que plus the perfect subjunctive. The men is nasal, and the final r gives the last syllable the stress: la-men-TAR.

example.target: Lamento muito que você tenha perdido o emprego.
example.source: I am very sorry that you lost your job.
example.source_literal: I-lament much that you have lost the job.

vocabulary.note: From proveito, benefit, so the idea is to get the benefit out of something such as a trip, time or a chance. Aproveite! is a common way of saying Enjoy it! The ei is a diphthong, the pr is a tap r after a consonant, and the final r puts the stress on the last syllable: a-pro-vei-TAR.

example.target: Ela aproveitou a viagem para conhecer os primos.
example.source: She took advantage of the trip to meet her cousins.
example.source_literal: She profited-from the trip to know the cousins.

vocabulary.note: The cedilla keeps the s sound before a (des-per-di-ÇAR). The d before i is said like j in jeans, and the final r puts the stress on the last syllable, so no accent is written.

example.target: Não quero desperdiçar essa oportunidade.
example.source: I don't want to waste this opportunity.

vocabulary.note: Con-se-QUÊN-ci-a: the final ia counts as two syllables, so the stress is on the third to last syllable and an accent is required; it is a circumflex because the e before n is closed. The u after q is pronounced like w (kw), one of the words that carried a trema before 2009, so the spelling does not show it. The en is nasal and c before i is s.

example.target: A chuva forte teve consequências graves para a cidade.
example.source: The heavy rain had serious consequences for the city.

vocabulary.note: The au is a diphthong said like ow in cow, and a single s between vowels is z: CAU-za. The pair causas e consequências is a common phrase in history writing.

example.target: A causa do acidente ainda não foi descoberta.
example.source: The cause of the accident has not been found yet.
example.source_literal: The cause of-the accident still not was discovered.

vocabulary.note: Followed by a noun, never by a clause: em consequência da greve. The de fuses with the article (de plus a gives da), as in the lesson on contractions. To link two clauses, use por isso instead. In the phrase, de is said like dji.

example.target: Em consequência da greve, muitos voos foram cancelados.
example.source: As a result of the strike, many flights were canceled.

vocabulary.note: Also means blame and guilt. An l that ends a syllable is said like w: KUW-pa. Ter culpa is to be at fault, and A culpa é minha is It's my fault.

example.target: A culpa não foi dele; ninguém tinha avisado sobre a mudança.
example.source: It wasn't his fault; nobody had told him about the change.
example.source_literal: The fault not was of-him; nobody had warned about the change.

vocabulary.note: In-FÂN-ci-a: the final ia counts as two syllables, so the stress is third to last and needs a mark. It is a circumflex because the a before n is closed and nasal, as in câmera. Portuguese says a infância where English says his childhood.

example.target: Ele passou a infância numa cidade pequena do interior.
example.source: He spent his childhood in a small town in the interior.
example.source_literal: He passed the childhood in-a city small of-the interior.

vocabulary.note: Ju-ven-TU-dji: the final e is said i, and d before that i is said like j in jeans. The stress is on tu, the second to last syllable, which the ending e predicts, so there is no accent. The en is nasal. Na juventude means in one's youth.

example.target: Na juventude, ela já sonhava em ser médica.
example.source: In her youth, she already dreamed of being a doctor.
example.source_literal: In-the youth, she already dreamed in to-be doctor.

vocabulary.note: The rr is the strong r and ei is a diphthong: ca-RREI-ra. The word also means a run or a race. Aposentar-se, to retire, is another reflexive verb.

example.target: Depois de vinte anos de carreira, ele resolveu se aposentar.
example.source: After a twenty-year career, he decided to retire.
example.source_literal: After of twenty years of career, he decided to retire-himself.

vocabulary.note: É-po-ca is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so it always carries an accent: acute because the e is open. C before o is k. Naquela época is at that time and nessa época is at this or that time; naquela is em plus aquela, as in the lesson on contractions.

example.target: Naquela época, poucas pessoas tinham telefone em casa.
example.source: At that time, few people had a telephone at home.
example.source_literal: In-that era, few people had telephone in house.

vocabulary.note: Im-PÉ-ri-o: the final io counts as two syllables, so the stress is third to last and needs the acute accent of an open e. The im is a nasal vowel, because the m ends the syllable before p.

example.target: O Brasil foi um império até mil oitocentos e oitenta e nove.
example.source: Brazil was an empire until 1889.
example.source_literal: The Brazil was an empire until thousand eight-hundred and eighty and nine.

vocabulary.note: Re-PÚ-bli-ca is stressed on the third to last syllable, so it always carries an accent, the same pattern as público from the stress lesson. The b and l stay together in one syllable.

example.target: A república foi proclamada no Brasil em mil oitocentos e oitenta e nove.
example.source: The republic was proclaimed in Brazil in 1889.

vocabulary.note: A-bo-li-ÇÃO: the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone is enough; it marks the nasal sound, and the stress is already on the last syllable by default. The cedilla keeps the s sound before a. The plural is abolições.

example.target: A abolição da escravidão aconteceu em mil oitocentos e oitenta e oito.
example.source: The abolition of slavery took place in 1888.

vocabulary.note: Same ending as abolição: i-mi-gra-ÇÃO. G before r is the hard g. Imigração is arriving in a country, emigração is leaving one; the two differ only in the first letter.

example.target: A imigração italiana mudou a paisagem cultural de São Paulo.
example.source: Italian immigration changed the cultural landscape of São Paulo.

vocabulary.note: From acontecer, to happen, plus -imento, the suffix that names the result of a verb. The stress is on men, the second to last syllable: a-con-te-ci-MEN-to. C before o is k and c before i is s; the on and en are nasal.

example.target: O jornal publicou uma lista dos principais acontecimentos do ano.
example.source: The newspaper published a list of the year's main events.

vocabulary.note: The thing given up follows de: desistir de fumar. The first s is between vowels and is said z, and the second s ends a syllable and is said s or sh by region: de-zis-TIR. The final r puts the stress on the last syllable.

example.target: Ela nunca desistiu do sonho de ser médica.
example.source: She never gave up on her dream of being a doctor.
example.source_literal: She never gave-up of-the dream of to-be doctor.

vocabulary.note: A formal and respectful alternative to morrer, used in news and obituaries. C before e is s, and the final r puts the stress on the last syllable: fa-le-CER. The eu of faleceu is a diphthong.

example.target: O escritor faleceu aos oitenta anos, cercado pela família.
example.source: The writer passed away at eighty, surrounded by his family.
example.source_literal: The writer passed-away at-the eighty years, surrounded by-the family.

vocabulary.note: Bolsa alone is a handbag or purse, and also a stock exchange; with de estudos it is money awarded to a student. The l that ends the first syllable is said like w: BOW-sa. Estudos is stressed on tu, as the ending os predicts.

example.target: Ele ganhou uma bolsa de estudos para estudar em Lisboa.
example.source: He won a scholarship to study in Lisbon.
example.source_literal: He won a bag of studies to study in Lisbon.

vocabulary.note: Also said olhando para trás, literally looking to back. The s before p ends a syllable and is said s or sh by region: re-tros-PEC-to, stressed on the second to last syllable as the ending o predicts.

example.target: Em retrospecto, eu teria tomado outra decisão.
example.source: In retrospect, I would have made another decision.

vocabulary.note: Por pouco não plus the preterite says that something almost happened, and it did not: Por pouco não perdi o trem means I almost missed the train, and I did not miss it. The não is real negation of the event that nearly occurred. The ou in pouco is a diphthong that often shrinks to a plain closed o.

example.target: Por pouco não perdi o último trem.
example.source: I almost missed the last train.
example.source_literal: For little not I-lost the last train.

vocabulary.note: A fixed phrase of relief about something that really happened, so the verb after que is in the indicative, not the subjunctive. The literal words do not explain the meaning; learn it as a unit. Ainda is a-IN-da: the i is stressed, so it is not a glide and the a stands in its own syllable, and the in is nasal. Bem ends in the nasal sound of em, like tem.

example.target: Ainda bem que você trouxe o guarda-chuva.
example.source: Thank goodness you brought the umbrella.
example.source_literal: Still well that you brought the umbrella.

vocabulary.note: Ao menos means at least, and ao is the contraction of a plus o from the lesson on prepositions, said like ow. Se ao menos plus the pluperfect subjunctive wishes that something past had been different; with the imperfect subjunctive it wishes about the present.

example.target: Se ao menos eu tivesse perguntado antes!
example.source: If only I had asked earlier!
example.source_literal: If at-the least I had asked before!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the verb forms of the compound tenses
grammar.explanation:
Every verb form in this unit is spelled by the two rules of the stress lesson. First, find the stressed syllable. Second, read the default for the way the word ends: words ending in a, e, o, am, em or ens (with or without a plural s) are stressed on the second to last syllable, and most other endings, including r, ei and ão, are stressed on the last. An accent is written only when the stress breaks that default, and it sits on the stressed vowel. The compound tenses make the rules easy to apply, because each is built from an auxiliary verb (ter or haver, the helper that carries the person and the tense) and a participle (the form that carries the meaning and, after ter, never changes). Only the auxiliary changes its ending, so only the auxiliary needs an accent explained; a participle is spelled from its infinitive.

Start with the imperfect of ter and haver, the auxiliary of the pluperfect. Tinha is TI-nha: the nh is one sound like ny in canyon, the t before i is said like ch in cheese (the position rule from the sounds lesson), and the ending a predicts second to last stress, so no accent is written. Tinham, they had, ends in am, which also predicts second to last stress, so it has no accent either; it is a different word from têm, they have, whose circumflex is the plural mark from the stress lesson. In tínhamos the ending -mos adds a syllable after the stressed one, so the stress falls on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts. A word stressed on the third to last syllable always carries an accent, so TÍ-nha-mos is written with an acute; the i has only one quality, so the mark shows stress and nothing else. Haver works the same way. Havia is ha-VI-a: the i is stressed and the a after it is a separate syllable, so the stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a, exactly as in tia. Havíamos is ha-VÍ-a-mos, third to last, so it needs the accent, like tínhamos.

The other auxiliaries differ only in where the stress falls. The future adds endings to the whole infinitive: terei is te-REI, with the diphthong ei stressed last, which is the default for ei, so no accent. Terá is stressed on the last syllable, but the ending a predicts the second to last, so the stress breaks the default and takes an acute, the same reasoning that gave você its circumflex. Terão is te-RÃO: ão is stressed last by default and the tilde marks the nasal sound. Teremos is te-RE-mos, second to last, which os predicts, so no mark. The conditional adds -ia: teria is te-RI-a, stressed on the i like tia, so no accent, and teríamos has one extra syllable and third to last stress, so it needs one, as gostaríamos did. The subjunctive auxiliaries come from the three subjunctive tenses. Tenha is TE-nha and tenhamos is te-NHA-mos, both second to last. Tivesse is ti-VES-se, with ss between vowels said s and the final e said i; tivéssemos has third to last stress, so it carries an acute, open because the irregular stem has an open e, as in the lesson on the imperfect subjunctive. Tiver ends in r, which predicts the last syllable, and tivermos ends in os, which predicts the second to last, so neither needs a mark.

The simple pluperfect shows the same pattern at the end of the word. The eles form of the preterite minus -ram plus -ra gives falara, fizera, fora and tivera: second to last stress with the ending a, so no accent. The nós form adds -mos and pushes the stress to the third to last syllable, so it is accented: faláramos, comêramos, partíramos, fizéramos, tivéramos, fôramos. The mark follows the vowel quality as always, acute for open vowels and circumflex for closed ones. The eles form, falaram, is spelled exactly like the preterite, so context tells you which tense it is.

Participles keep the spelling of their stem: feito, dito, visto, escrito, aberto and posto. The one accent that matters is the í of saído. Sa-Í-do has a hiatus: the a and the stressed i do not glide into one syllable, and a stressed i or u that is the second vowel of a hiatus is written with the accent when it is alone in its syllable or followed only by s, as in saúde and país. Followed by any other consonant it takes no accent (juiz, ruim). Compare partido (par-TI-do), where the i follows a consonant and needs nothing. Construído follows the same rule with u and í. The letters follow the sounds lesson too: the d of dito is said like j in jeans, because it comes before i.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of regret, history and life stories
grammar.explanation:
The nouns and phrases of this unit belong to the vocabulary of memory, regret and history, and a few rules explain nearly every mark in them. The method is the one from the stress lesson: divide the word into syllables, find the stress, read the default for the ending, and compare.

The first rule is that a word stressed on the third to last syllable always carries an accent, because no ending predicts it: época, música, ótimo, século, república, máquinas. The second rule extends it. The endings -ia, -io, -ea and -eo count as two syllables in the spelling, even though in speech they are often said as one quick beat, so a word such as infância (in-FÂN-ci-a), consequência, experiência, história (his-TÓ-ri-a), império (im-PÉ-ri-o), prêmio, sério, vários, férias and Áurea (ÁU-re-a, in Lei Áurea) is stressed on the third to last syllable and needs a mark. The test is where you hear the stress. If it falls on the syllable before ia or io, write the accent. If it falls on the i itself, as in cronologia (cro-no-lo-GI-a), teria and tia, the stress is on the second to last syllable, which the ending a predicts, and no accent is written.

The choice between acute and circumflex is the quality of the vowel: acute for open (época, história, império, sério, férias), circumflex for closed (prêmio). Before an m or n in the middle of a word the vowel is nasalized and is written with the circumflex by convention, as in câmera and Antônio from the stress lesson: infância and consequência have â and ê for that reason. Words in -ão keep the tilde: abolição, imigração, escravidão, multidão. The cedilla in ç gives the s sound before a, o and u, and the plural of -ção is -ções (invenções); other words in -ão often take -ões too (versões), with the tilde on the o.

Several letter patterns come from the sounds lesson. Qu before e or i normally has a silent u (esqueci, máquinas, Henrique), but in a few words the u is pronounced like w: consequência, frequência and cinquenta. Since the spelling reform of 2009 no trema marks them, so you learn which words they are. A gu before e or i is also normally silent (seguinte, ninguém), while gu before a is pronounced, as in Guarujá (gwa-ru-JÁ). Ninguém is an oxytone ending in em, which needs an accent, exactly like também. A single s between vowels is z (causa, Isabel), ss is s (assinada, promessa, discussões), and sc is s (nasceu). An l at the end of a syllable is said like w (culpa, bolsa, mil, talvez). In most of Brazil, t and d before the i sound, including a final e said i, become ch and j: tinha, juventude (ju-ven-TU-dji), cidade, de. G before e or i and the letter j are both the sound in measure: viagem, energia, Gerais. Nh and lh are single sounds (senhor, linha, escolha, milhares), rr is the strong r (arrependimento, carreira), and r after n is also strong (Henrique). The x of ex before a vowel is z (exatamente), and x before a consonant is s (experiência, said es-pe-ri-ÊN-cia).

Two more cases connect to the grammar. Saí and saído have the hiatus accent explained in the previous note. And the numbers in dates need two marks: três is a stressed one-syllable word ending in es, which takes an accent, and dezoito and dezenove have z between vowels. In ainda, the i is stressed, so it is not a glide beside the a: a-IN-da, with a nasal in. Treat the table as a checklist: when a new word has an accent, count the syllables, find the stress and compare it with the default, instead of memorizing the word.

grammar.title: The pluperfect: a past before a past
grammar.explanation:
Every tense places an event in time relative to a reference point. The simple preterite (fui, comi) uses the present moment as its reference point: the event is before now. The pluperfect needs two points. It talks about an event that was already complete before a second, earlier moment in the past, so it is a past of the past. The name says so: pluperfect comes from Latin for more than perfect, further back than the ordinary past, and the Portuguese name, mais-que-perfeito, translates it word for word. The second moment can be a time (às oito), another event (quando cheguei) or a point understood from the story. English builds the same idea with had plus a participle, and Portuguese does it in the same way.

A compound tense is an auxiliary verb plus a participle, as the lesson on the present compound explained. The pluperfect uses ter in the imperfect, tinha, with the participle: tinha falado, tinha feito, tinha ido. Each part has a job. The imperfect puts the viewpoint in the past, in the setting of the story, and the participle says that the action was complete from that viewpoint. Ter carries the person (tinha, tínhamos, tinham) and the participle never changes: it does not agree with the subject (Elas tinham saído, not saídas), because after ter the participle is part of the verb and not a describing adjective. Já, ainda não and nunca go before ter: Eu nunca tinha visto o mar. A pronoun goes between ter and the participle in speech (ele tinha me avisado) and before the auxiliary in formal writing after a negative word (ninguém os havia lido).

This tense is broader than its present-tense twin. The present compound (tenho feito) covers only repeated or continuing action up to now, because a finished event is told with the preterite. In the past, no ordinary simple tense competes for the job of saying before that other past moment, so tinha feito has every use of English had done: a single completed event (Ele já tinha saído), an experience (Nunca tinha visto uma cidade tão grande), or the reason behind a past situation (A culpa não foi dele; ninguém tinha avisado).

Compare three sentences with the same opening. Quando cheguei, ele saiu: he left after I arrived, the preterite continuing a chain of events. Quando cheguei, ele estava saindo: he was in the middle of leaving as I arrived, the imperfect progressive describing the background. Quando cheguei, ele já tinha saído: he had left before I arrived and was already gone, the pluperfect looking back from the reference point. The tense is chosen by how the event relates to the reference point: after it, during it or before it. When the order is already clear from antes de, depois que or the order of the sentences, Portuguese is content to use the preterite for both events (Depois que ele saiu, eu cheguei); the pluperfect is for when the earlier event would otherwise be unclear, or when you step back to explain.

The auxiliary can also be haver, as in havia falado and havíamos falado. The meaning is identical; haver is the formal choice of newspapers, history books and written Portuguese, while ter is what people say. The note on regret and the compound infinitive compares the two. Portuguese also has a simple pluperfect, one word with no auxiliary: falara. It comes from Latin and is built from the eles form of the preterite: remove -ram and add -ra, -ra, -ramos, -ram. Falaram gives falara, fizeram gives fizera, foram gives fora, tiveram gives tivera and disseram gives dissera, so irregular stems carry through, the same recipe that gave the future subjunctive and the imperfect subjunctive. The form survives in literary writing and in a few fixed phrases. One you already know is quem me dera: dera is the simple pluperfect of dar, so the phrase literally says who to-me had-given. Fora is the pluperfect of both ser and ir, because foram is the preterite of both; it is spelled exactly like the word fora, outside (lá fora), and context settles which one you are reading. Use tinha plus participle yourself, and recognize the simple form when you read.

You have already met the pluperfect in reported speech, where the preterite becomes the pluperfect after a past reporting verb (Fui ao médico becomes Ela disse que tinha ido ao médico). In casual speech Brazilians often leave the order of events to context and the word já, so you will also hear Ele já saiu quando eu cheguei. Standard writing keeps the pluperfect, and it is always safe.

grammar.title: One recipe for every compound tense: the future perfect and the conditional perfect
grammar.explanation:
Once you know that a compound tense is an auxiliary plus a participle, the whole family of this unit follows from one recipe: put ter in the tense that sets the viewpoint, and add the participle to say that the action is complete from that viewpoint. Ter in the imperfect gives the pluperfect, complete before a point in the past. Ter in the future gives the future perfect, complete before a point in the future. Ter in the conditional gives the conditional perfect, which is would have done. The three subjunctive tenses give three more, in the next note. Nothing else changes: the participle is fixed and ter supplies the person. The table collects the family.

The future perfect (futuro do presente composto) is ter in the future plus a participle: terei feito, terá feito, teremos feito, terão feito. It says that an action will already be complete when a future moment arrives: Até sexta, terei terminado o relatório. English also says will have done, but with a difference in the time clause: English says By the time you wake up, I will have left, with a present tense after by the time. Portuguese uses the future subjunctive in that clause, as in every quando clause: Quando você acordar, eu já terei saído. The word já makes the completion plain. The tense is formal. In everyday speech Brazilians build it with ir: Até sexta eu já vou ter terminado, literally I-go to-have finished. Ter terminado is the infinitive of ter plus a participle, called the compound infinitive, which means to have finished and is taught fully in the note on regret.

The future perfect has a second job: a guess about the past, where English says must have or will have. Ele já terá chegado means He has probably arrived by now. This use is formal; in speech people say Ele já deve ter chegado, using dever as in the probability lesson (deve ser) with the compound infinitive.

The conditional perfect (futuro do pretérito composto) is ter in the conditional plus a participle: teria feito, teríamos feito, teriam feito, meaning would have done. The conditional itself, as the earlier lessons showed, is the form of imagined events (viajaria, would travel); the compound moves the imagined event into the past, so viajaria becomes teria viajado. It has four uses. First, it is the result clause of an unreal past condition, taught in the next note: Se eu tivesse sabido, teria ido. Second, it appears when the condition is left unsaid: Eu teria ido, mas estava doente. Third, it is what the future perfect becomes in reported speech after a past verb, following the backshift rule from the reported speech unit: Ela disse que, até sexta, teria terminado. Fourth, in journalism it presents a fact as reported but unconfirmed: O ministro teria dito que vai renunciar. The logic is the same as for the conditional in general: the form signals distance, here distance from certainty, so the newspaper reports the statement without vouching for it. In speech the imperfect often replaces the conditional perfect: Se eu tivesse sabido, eu ia, using ia from ir, literally I was going.

Do not confuse the real with the imagined. Tinha ido says that he went; teria ido says that he would have gone, but did not, or that the report is unconfirmed. The auxiliary tense decides.

grammar.title: Compound subjunctive tenses and unreal past conditions
grammar.explanation:
The subjunctive, as the earlier lessons showed, presents an event as wished for, doubted, imagined or not yet real, and Portuguese has three subjunctive tenses: the present (fale), the imperfect (falasse) and the future (falar). Each one has a compound partner, built by the recipe of the last note: ter in that subjunctive tense plus the participle. The present subjunctive tenha gives the perfect subjunctive tenha feito, the imperfect tivesse gives the pluperfect subjunctive tivesse feito, and the future tiver gives the future perfect subjunctive tiver feito. The compound adds one idea to the subjunctive: the event is complete. The choice among the three is made by the same things as for the simple tenses, the time of the main verb and how real the situation is.

The perfect subjunctive follows a trigger in the present and refers to something already done: Espero que ele tenha chegado, Duvido que ela tenha dito isso, Não acho que ele tenha entendido, É possível que eles tenham saído, Embora tenha estudado muito, ela não passou. Compare the simple present subjunctive, which looks ahead: Espero que ele chegue (he has not arrived yet). The pluperfect subjunctive is the same idea seen from the past or from an imagined point: Esperava que ele tivesse chegado is a past hope, and above all it is the condition in an unreal past sentence. The future perfect subjunctive says that something will be done before another future moment: Assim que tiver terminado, eu te aviso. It also follows se for an open possibility that is complete: Se ele tiver estudado, vai passar. Often the simple future subjunctive does the same job (Assim que terminar, te aviso), and the compound is chosen to stress that one action must be finished first.

Now the conditions of the earlier unit, in which three degrees of reality were distinguished. A condition about the past that did not happen cannot be changed, so it is unreal in the strongest way, and Portuguese uses the unreal pair in its compound form: Se eu tivesse sabido (pluperfect subjunctive) goes with teria ido (conditional perfect). English uses the same pair, had known and would have gone, so the structures match exactly. The English slip If I would have known must not be copied: after se, the verb is never a conditional. Both clauses are compound because both the condition and the result lie in the past. If the result is in the present, only the if-clause is compound: Se você tivesse aceitado, teria uma vida bem diferente hoje, where teria is the simple conditional of ter, would have. That is the sentence Fernanda says in the first dialogue. If the past fact is simply not known to be false, use the indicative: Se ele já saiu, não adianta ir.

The same tense appears wherever an imagined or regretted past is expressed. Se ao menos tivesse perguntado! is a se clause standing alone. Quem me dera ter ido uses the compound infinitive, because the wisher is also the one who would have gone. After como se it describes an imagined past: Ela chorou como se tivesse perdido tudo. After talvez it gives a past possibility that did not happen: Talvez eu não tivesse conhecido tanta gente boa, maybe I would not have met so many good people. Quem sabe, literally who knows, works like talvez: Quem sabe eu já tenha aprendido uma música inteira. And tomara que follows the line from the earlier lessons between the possible and the remote: Tomara que tenha dado certo hopes for something that may have happened, while Tomara que tivesse dado certo wishes it had, knowing it did not. In speech the result clause often uses the imperfect (Se eu tivesse sabido, eu ia), but the se clause keeps tivesse.

grammar.title: Regret and missed chances: the compound infinitive, devia ter and ter or haver
grammar.explanation:
The plain infinitive is the form of the verb with no person and no tense, and it needs another verb or a preposition to hang on. Ter plus a participle makes the compound infinitive (infinitivo composto): ter feito, to have done. It is how Portuguese says that an action is complete when no tense can be used: devia ter feito, depois de ter terminado, sem ter dito nada, lamento ter demorado. In these examples ter stays in the plain infinitive and does not change; the person is carried by the first verb. When the second verb has its own subject, ter can take the personal infinitive endings from the earlier unit: depois de termos terminado, after we finished.

To say should have or could have, Portuguese stacks two layers: devia (the imperfect of dever, to owe or must) or podia (the imperfect of poder, to be able) plus the compound infinitive. The first layer puts the obligation or the possibility in the past, and the second layer says that the act itself was not carried out: Eu devia ter estudado mais, Você podia ter avisado. Without ter the meaning shifts to the present or future: Eu devia estudar mais says I should study more from now on, and Você podia começar agora says you could start now. The conditional forms deveria ter and poderia ter mean the same, slightly more polite and formal. The question to ask is whether the act belongs to the past, in which case add ter, or to the present and future, in which case do not. English has the same logic in should have and could have, but hides the compound inside have; Portuguese keeps ter visible.

Other patterns of regret and relief use the same pieces. With the same subject, an infinitive: Me arrependo de não ter ido, Lamento não ter aproveitado melhor a juventude. With a different subject, que plus the perfect subjunctive, because the event is something the speaker feels about but does not assert: Lamento que você tenha perdido o emprego, Que pena que ele não tenha vindo. Relief is different: Ainda bem que plus the indicative, because you are celebrating a fact that really happened: Ainda bem que você veio. Por pouco não plus the preterite says that something almost happened, and the não is real negation: Por pouco não perdi o trem means I almost missed the train, and I did not miss it. The phrase is literally for little not I-lost.

All the compound tenses can use ter or haver as the auxiliary. The two verbs come from different Latin verbs: haver from habere, to have, which was the original auxiliary in Portuguese (the old hei feito), and ter from tenere, to hold, which is the origin the present compound lesson described with tenho a carta escrita. Over the centuries ter replaced haver in speech, and in the present compound only ter is used today. Haver remains as a formal alternative in the tenses that are mostly written: havia feito, haverá feito, houvesse feito. The meaning is identical; only the register changes. Haver is also the impersonal verb there is and there was from the lesson on tem and há: há, havia, houve, haverá. The form is the same, and the participle tells you which one you are reading: Havia muita gente na festa, there were many people, has no participle; Os convidados já haviam saído, the guests had already left, has one. They also behave differently. The impersonal haver stays singular even with a plural noun (Havia muitas pessoas, never haviam), while the auxiliary agrees with its subject (As pessoas haviam saído).

grammar.title: Telling a life story or history: layers of time
grammar.explanation:
A life story or a stretch of history is a narrative, and a narrative has layers of time. The main line is the chain of events, each after the one before. The background is what the setting was like and what used to happen. And an earlier layer is what had already happened before the main line reached that point. Portuguese gives each layer its own tense: the preterite for events on the main line (Nasci em Recife, Saí de casa, ganhei um prêmio), the imperfect for the background and for habits (Meu pai era carpinteiro), and the pluperfect for the earlier layer (Aos dez anos eu já tinha escrito meu primeiro conto). A fourth layer is the unreal, which uses the pluperfect subjunctive and the conditional perfect to ask what would have happened otherwise: Se eu tivesse desistido, não teria chegado onde cheguei.

Time markers keep the layers clear. Years are said as full numbers in words, with em: em mil novecentos e seis, literally in thousand nine-hundred and six, with no short form like nineteen oh six. Decades and centuries use de or no and a cardinal number: na década de sessenta, no século dezenove, literally in-the century nineteen, where English uses an ordinal, nineteenth century. Ages use aos plus the number: aos dezoito anos, literally at-the eighteen years, which is a plus os from the lesson on contractions. Periods of life take na: na infância, na juventude. Order is signalled by antes disso, depois disso, no ano seguinte (the following year), naquela época and nessa época (at that time, from em plus aquela or essa) and até então (until then). The words já, ainda não and nunca tell the listener that a pluperfect is coming.

Cause and consequence tie the events together. A causa is what produces an event, and a consequência is what follows from it. Em consequência de takes a noun (em consequência da abolição), while two clauses need another link such as por isso, that is why: A greve começou, por isso muitos voos foram cancelados. The pluperfect also often supplies the cause: when an earlier event explains a later one, it is natural to look back with tinha plus a participle, as in O voo atrasou porque a tempestade tinha fechado o aeroporto.

In writing about history Brazilian authors often prefer havia to tinha, and in literary works you may meet the simple pluperfect (fora, dissera). The structure is the same in every register; only the auxiliary changes.

culture.title: Arrependimento, saudade e a sabedoria dos provérbios
culture.text:
Brazilians have many sayings about regret and hindsight, and each rewards a word-for-word reading. Não adianta chorar o leite derramado says literally it does not advance to cry the spilled milk, and means that it is useless to cry over spilled milk. Depois de casa roubada, trancas na porta says after of house robbed, bolts on-the door, the local version of locking the barn door after the horse has gone. Água passada não move moinho says water passed does not move mill: water that has already gone by cannot turn the mill wheel, so the past cannot be changed. Each one invites a compound tense in the comment that follows: Eu devia ter trancado a porta, Se ao menos tivesse ouvido.

A uniquely Brazilian word in this field is saudade, the mix of nostalgia and longing for a person, a place or a time. Songs, poems and everyday talk use it constantly: Que saudade daquela época! says literally what longing of-that era. The pluperfect is natural here, because saudade looks back at a time that had already ended. Brazil is also a country of life stories: biographies of athletes, musicians and politicians sell well, and television programs often reconstruct a famous person's career through family interviews.

The greatest Brazilian master of the literary past tenses is Machado de Assis, whose novel Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas (literally posthumous memoirs of Brás Cubas), published in 1881, is narrated by a dead man who tells his life story with irony. In books like this one you will find the simple pluperfect (fora, dissera, tivera), which is now rare in speech. When you read Brazilian history, from the arrival of the royal court in 1808 to the republic in 1889, you will find chronology told with exactly the tenses studied here, often with havia instead of tinha.
